t: LeetCode 1681 — Minimum Incompatibility: Canonical Bitmask Groups and Subset DP
o:
Partition n (at most 16) numbers into k subsets of equal size m = n/k, each subset free of duplicates, minimizing the total of per-subset max - min.

Example 1: [1, 2, 1, 4] splits as [1, 2] + [1, 4] costing (2-1) + (4-1) = 4 - the tempting [1,1] + [2,4] is illegal because of the repeated 1. Example 2 reaches 6 with four pairs. Example 3 is impossible: value 3 appears four times but only k = 3 subsets exist, so by pigeonhole any value whose frequency exceeds k dooms the split.

The tiny n invites bitmask techniques: enumerate candidate groups as masks, then combine them with subset DP, always seeding each new group from the lowest unused index so no partition is ever counted twice.
k: Feasibility is pure pigeonhole: if any value occurs more than k times, return -1 immediately.
After sorting, a group’s incompatibility is lastChosenValue minus firstChosenValue - computable per mask in one pass.
Always grow the next group from the lowest unused index; this canonical choice makes the DP visit every partition exactly once.

a.n: Approach 1: Sorted Backtracking with Symmetry Pruning
a.i: Place values in ascending order; each element joins any open group that lacks its value or opens a new group. Appending sorted values grows a group span incrementally (x minus the previous last element), so costs update in O(1). Skipping structurally identical groups at one depth kills most of the symmetric blowup, and pruning against the incumbent best trims the rest.
s: Sort nums; bail out immediately if some value appears more than k times.
Recursion places nums[i] into each distinct compatible open group, or into a fresh group while fewer than k are open.
Span delta when appending x to a group currently ending at y is x - y (zero for an empty group).
Deduplicate identical group states per call and prune when accumulated total already reaches the best found.
Record the best total once all n elements are placed.
a.t: Exponential in the worst case — bounded by pruned placements of n elements into k groups
a.sp: O(n) — recursion depth plus the stored group contents

a.n: Approach 2: Bitmask DP with Precomputed Group Costs
a.i: Precompute cost[mask] for every size-m mask whose selected values are pairwise distinct. dp[mask] is the cheapest way to have consumed exactly the elements of mask; expand each reachable state only through the group containing its lowest free index, enumerating submasks of the remaining free bits and keeping those that form valid groups. The work sums to the classic 3^n submask-enumeration bound - comfortable at n = 16.
s: Sort; reject when a value frequency exceeds k; build a popcount table.
For every mask of popcount m whose selected values are distinct, set cost[mask] = maxValue - minValue.
dp[0] = 0; for each reachable mask let i be its lowest free index.
Enumerate submasks sub of the other free bits with popcount m - 1; relax dp[mask | sub | 1<<i] with dp[mask] + cost[...].
a.t: O(3^n) — summing 2^(free bits) over all states gives the submask bound; n <= 16 keeps it fast
a.sp: O(2^n) — dp, cost, and popcount tables

w:
Open with the pigeonhole check - it resolves impossibility instantly and shows you understand when the answer is -1.
Hazards: forgetting groups must be exactly size m, double-counting permuted groups (the lowest-free-index seed fixes both), and enumerating every submask without the popcount filter, which multiplies work needlessly.
Likely follow-ups: maximize the sum instead of minimizing, weight each element, or process the array in streaming batches where only the DP version extends naturally.
